paras: The lynching of Cal Emory took place about midnight on the night of June 13, 1881, when about twenty-five armed men forced the county jail at Dover, Pope County, Arkansas, shot Emory in his cell and hanged him on a gallows. Emory had been convicted of murdering a woman in Franklin County and sentenced to death, but Governor Churchill had commuted the sentence to twenty-one years in the penitentiary a few weeks earlier. It was the third attempt to lynch him, and Arkansas papers largely excused it as a rebuke to the governor's pardons.

Emory, of Franklin County, was convicted of murder at the September 1880 term of the Pope County circuit court on a change of venue. His appeal was still pending when, in early June, the governor commuted the sentence on a petition from Franklin County and a judge of the supreme court. A wire item in the Daily Republican said Emory and James Youngblood had "feloniously assaulted and murdered" his betrothed, Mary E. Taylor, in Franklin County nearly a year earlier, and that Youngblood had also received clemency. No report states the race of Emory, of the woman or of the men who killed him.

The Russellville Democrat called the commutation "an outrage upon public decency." Early on Friday, June 10, during a storm, a party of armed men tried without success to break open the Dover jail, in what a Gazette special to the Memphis Appeal described as an attempt to lynch Emory. Later reports counted the fatal raid as the third attempt.

About midnight on Monday, June 13, the lynchers forced the jail and overpowered the guards. According to a letter signed "Citizen," the men smoked the jailer out of the upper story, threw a blanket over him and sat on him. When one of them started down a ladder into the cell, Emory broke a round from the ladder and drove him back.

The men tried to make a fellow prisoner, called "a negro prisoner," put the rope on Emory; the accounts differ on whether he did. Emory was then shot in the head, taken from the jail and hanged on the gallows the sheriff had built for his lawful execution. Accounts agreed he was dead or nearly so when hanged, and the body hung until the coroner arrived late Tuesday evening.

The Gazette special and the Russellville Democrat said the lynchers came from Franklin County and were friends of the murdered woman. Answering a "Citizen" letter that placed "the stain" on Pope County, the Democrat said there was no evidence any Pope County citizen took part. No report of a coroner's verdict, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage; one item noted that Arkansas authorities had not moved to punish any of the month's lynchers.

The Little Rock Gazette's Russellville special ran out of state on June 14 and 15, from Memphis and Rock Island to Nevada and Sacramento. Headlines included "Summary Justice In Arkansaw," "Got Him at Last," "A Reversed Decision" and "Determined Vigilantes," and the wire called Emory "the wife murderer." Weekly digests garbled the details, moving the lynching to Russellville or "Denver, Ark." and renaming the victim "Al Emory" or "Carl Emery."

Arkansas commentary mostly excused the killing and blamed the governor. Among exchanges reprinted by the Russellville Democrat, the Atkins News said it was "willing to see all men who commit rapes, hung without judge or jury," and the Independent Arkansian said Emory "got his just deserts." The Hot Springs Sentinel, quoted in the Public Ledger, called the lynching "the reproof of an indignant community" against the governor's abuse of the pardoning power. The Public Ledger, which had called the raiders "a quiet, orderly mob," wrote that the method was "not commendable" but welcomed the result. The main dissent came from the "Citizen" letter, which called the affair "greatly to be deplored."

Accounts differed on whether the woman was Emory's wife, as the wire said, or his betrothed. Several papers, though not the wire, said she was also raped, and the Independent Arkansian said her body was thrown into Mulberry Creek. The Russellville Democrat described the conviction first as for murder and later as for two capital crimes.

accounts.gist: Twenty-five armed men, thought to be Franklin County friends of the murdered woman, took the Dover jail and hanged Emory, who resisted and was shot in the head; it was the third attempt.

accounts.label: Russellville Democrat (local paper)
accounts.gist: After a failed Friday attempt, the lynchers forced the jail Monday about midnight, shot Emory, had a fellow prisoner adjust a noose, hanged him on a gallows and left the body until the coroner came.

accounts.label: 'Citizen' letter to the Little Rock Democrat
accounts.gist: The jailer was smoked out and held down; Emory fought off a man on a ladder and was shot three or four times, then hanged dead on the sheriff's gallows; the stain rests on Pope County.

accounts.label: Daily Republican wire flash
accounts.gist: An armed mob of twenty-five lynched Emory, who with James Youngblood had assaulted and murdered his betrothed, Mary E. Taylor.

framing.detail: Log Cabin, Atkins News, Van Buren Graphic and Independent Arkansian excused the lynching and blamed executive clemency; Ozark Democrat regretted mob law but expected it.
Memphis Public Ledger headlined 'Summary Justice In Arkansaw' and editorially called the method not commendable but the result welcome.
Hot Springs Sentinel called it 'the reproof of an indignant community' against Churchill.
Russellville Democrat condemned the commutation, reported the lynching flatly, and denied any stain on Pope County.
'Citizen' letter called the affair 'greatly to be deplored' and said the stain rested on Pope County.
Out-of-state dailies ran the wire under heads such as 'Got Him at Last' and 'A Reversed Decision'; weekly digests made it a 'neck-tie sociable'.

conflicts.note: The local Russellville Democrat consistently prints 'Cal Emory'; the others are wire or digest variants.
Russellville was the dateline of the Gazette special; the local accounts place the jail at Dover.
The local paper and the June 14 dispatches agree on Monday night; the Tuesday version is a later digest.
No local Arkansas account calls her his wife; the Russellville Democrat says only 'a woman'.
The Russellville Democrat said on June 9 he was convicted of murder and on June 23 that he was sentenced for two capital crimes.
Most reports, including the local paper, say twenty-one years.
